title: Executive Presence: Own the Room, Be Heard, Get Credit
author: Ethan Evans
source: Level Up with Ethan Evans (levelupwithethanevans.substack.com), June 30, 2026
summary: Ethan Evans (with co-author Jason) argues that hard work alone does not earn recognition or promotion — executives promote people whose impact is visible — and that executive presence, far from being an innate personality trait, is the outcome of multiple controllable inputs that can be learned and practiced: preparation, reputation, clarity, confidence, meeting control, follow-up, body language, empowering others, and composure under pressure. He emphasizes that gravitas — the weight of reputation, judgment, and a visible body of work — matters even more than polished speaking, and that executives, being busy, want the answer first: lead with the conclusion using frameworks like BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front), 'be bright, be quick, be gone,' and 'What / So What / Now What.' Specificity creates credibility — concrete numbers, timelines and tradeoffs land where general language fails — and, drawing on coach John Wooden's emphasis on habit built through repetition, Evans shows through live role-plays that presence improves quickly with direct feedback and real practice.
points: Hard work is table stakes: executives promote people whose impact is visible and connected to business priorities, not simply those working hardest.
Executive presence is not one innate trait but the outcome of controllable, learnable inputs — preparation, clarity, confidence, meeting control, body language and more.
Gravitas — the weight of reputation, judgment and a visible body of work — matters even more than polished speaking, because it earns the right to be heard.
Lead with the answer: use BLUF (Bottom Line Up Front), 'be bright, be quick, be gone,' and 'What / So What / Now What' to state conclusion, stakes and recommendation.
Specificity creates credibility, and presence improves quickly with direct feedback and repeated practice under pressure, echoing John Wooden's emphasis on built habits.
quotes: Hard work is table stakes. It matters, but it does not automatically lead to recognition, influence, or promotion.
Executive presence is often treated like a vague personality trait, but it is a combination of specific behaviors you can learn and practice
Gravitas is the weight of your reputation, judgment, and body of work. People listen more closely when they believe you have earned the right to speak.
Executives are busy. They do not want a long journey through your thinking before you arrive at the point.
When they added specific numbers, business outcomes, timelines, tradeoffs, and risks, their message immediately improved.
Executive presence is a learnable skill, but it requires practice under pressure, honest feedback, and repetition.
